1:
Why the description runs upward rather than down is answered two ways. Adam Clarke notes that the previous chapter praised her from head to foot, so this is a new description in reverse order, and reads the opening clause as praise of her walking: the sandals of Eastern women are richly embroidered, and the majestic walk of a woman so shod is peculiarly grand — which he thinks is why she is called a prince's daughter at once. Charles Ellicott connects the order with the dance named at the end of the previous chapter, since a dancer's feet would draw the eye first, and quotes a verse on the bride from the arch of her feet to the crest on her shining head. John Gill supplies precedent from Homer on the beautiful feet of one goddess and the golden shoes of another, and from Herodotus that an Egyptian city was assigned to the queen to keep her in shoes.

The title itself is taken at different depths. Keil and Delitzsch derive the noun from nobility of disposition before nobility of birth, and say Shulamith is so called because she has been raised to the rank of which Hannah's song speaks, her beauty joined to unaffected dignity. Matthew Henry applies the title wholly to the Church, a prince's daughter by new birth and by marriage: Christ found her mean and despicable and by betrothing her made her what she is called.

The figures that follow are variously taken as body or as dress. Gill reports that some understand not the navel but a covering for it, a jewel or plate of gold, and passes on a bishop's opinion that the clothing of wrought gold is meant, embossed with sheaves of wheat and bordered with embroidered lilies. Clarke agrees that ornamental dress about the loins is likely, grounding the judgment on hundreds of decorated Asiatic drawings in his own collection. Ellicott explains the wheat from a traveller's account of Syria, where the colour of wheat is thought the most beautiful a human body can have and winnowed heaps are decorated with flowers in token of harvest joy.

On the neck and after, the interest is topographical. Delitzsch takes the article before ivory to point to a particular tower faced with ivory tablets, well known around Jerusalem, since otherwise the place would have been specified as in the next comparison. Ellicott corrects the fishpools to pools simply, our version having followed the Latin without authority, and reports that the ruins of Heshbon keep the ancient name and that a photograph of the spring-head had lately been published by the Palestine exploration society. Clarke is candid about the next comparison: there was doubtless a propriety in likening the nose to a tower which cannot now be discerned. Wesley locates Heshbon beyond Jordan and supposes the tower a watch-tower built by Solomon on the northern border toward Damascus.

The last verse turns on a single word. Ellicott reports that the margin gives crimson instead of Carmel, from a pointing which better preserves the parallel with the purple of the next clause, but prefers the mountain, since the passage deals in figures drawn from places and a well-set head is as aptly likened to a mountain as a nose to a tower; a play on words may be intended. Delitzsch keeps the mountain and explains the idiom that the head is upon her, a man being thought of as the central unity of the members that make up his appearance; Shulamith's head ruled her form as Carmel ruled the land and sea at its feet, and Muslim poets like to compare hair to long leaves. Clarke renders the closing clause that the king is detained in the antechamber, his heart captivated; Wesley has him unable to look away once he has seen her.
6:
The exclamation opening the passage is read as general truth by one commentator and as address by the rest. Keil and Delitzsch call it a saying of all-embracing application: nothing is more admirable than the uniting of two lives, the one giving itself to the other and so finding its own complement, a self-devotion that is at the same time self-enrichment. John Gill keeps the speaker in view, hearing the King in the galleries wonder at a beauty which could not be said how great it was. John Wesley refers the delights to the lovely features in her.

The palm carries the next comparison, and each writer takes a different feature of the tree. Gill argues from the word for stature, which properly means height and erectness, that tallness was reckoned agreeable in women as well as men, citing the poets who likened one beauty to a plane tree and another to a cypress. Delitzsch adds that the Arabians call the palm's leaf-branches the sisters of men, and hears in the following clause the vine that climbs the house wall, an emblem of the housewife. Charles Ellicott observes that the tree's name was itself common as a woman's name. Wesley thinks the palm chosen because it is constantly green and grows upward in spite of all pressures.

Whether the clusters are grapes or dates is settled the same way twice. Adam Clarke states flatly that dates are the fruit of the palm and grow in clusters, and that it is these and not grapes which are meant. Ellicott reaches the same result from the printing: the supplied words were probably added by the English translators to agree with the clusters of the vine following, though the rich date clusters are in the poet's thought.

On climbing the tree Gill is the naturalist, reporting from Pliny that the bark carries rings like steps by which easterners ascend with incredible swiftness, and from Dr Shaw that the knots left by lopped boughs serve as rungs of a ladder. Clarke passes on without comment that the rubric in his old manuscript interprets the ascent of the cross of Christ. Ellicott works on the words: the term for boughs occurs only here and is probably formed from the sound, denoting the waving of the feathery branches; and nose stands for breath apparently because its root resembles that of the word for apple.

The wine of the ninth verse is taken for speech by most and for a textual problem by one. Gill allows taste, or breath, or, as he prefers, her speech, warming and comforting in conversation. Clarke makes it the voice: as good wine loosens the most backward tongue, so hearing her makes the taciturn eloquent. Wesley has the dull and sleepy made to speak. Ellicott holds that the text has evidently undergone change: the Greek read lips and teeth where ours has lips of sleepers, the margin reads the ancient, which Luther renders of the previous year, and the words for my beloved are either a copyist's insertion caught from the next verse or wrongly pointed. As it stands, he says, the verse is untranslatable.

The closing verse is placed rather than expounded. Ellicott notes that it ends a section rather than beginning one. Delitzsch misses the answering clause found earlier in the book and derives the word for desire from a root meaning to impel, the impulse of love as a natural power, referring it to the sentence on the woman in Genesis. Clarke marks the same word and reads that sentence reversed: what was part of the curse is here the bride's boast, his desire being upon her. His old manuscript renders it that she is to her love, and to her the turning of him. Matthew Henry hears the church triumphing in her relation to Christ, not her own but wholly devoted to him.
11:
The invitation to go into the field divides the commentators by what scene is being staged. Keil and Delitzsch report that Hitzig opens a new scene here, headed with Shulamith hastening home with her lover, and that on the shepherd hypothesis the bride shakes her head at the king's praise and calls to the absent shepherd instead, Ewald making this conceivable by supposing her lifted in spirit above the present, half here and half already in her rural home. Delitzsch answers that nothing is more incredible than such a Shulamith. Adam Clarke stays with domestic circumstance, on the conjecture that the bridegroom rose early each morning and withdrew to the country, leaving the bride asleep with orders that she not be disturbed; here she asks to go with him.

Two read the words as the church's. John Gill hears her calling Christ to make good his promise, an earnest desire which grows the more it is enjoyed, and a confession that visiting the congregations would come to little unless he went with her; Christ is not unwilling, he adds, but chooses to seem so, that his people may prize his presence the more. John Wesley is briefer: they retire from the crowd to converse more freely. Charles Ellicott hears a reminiscence of the courtship in the woodland places, and passes on the conjecture that the verse suggested Milton's line about the morrow ere fresh morning streaks the east.

Early rising is grammar to one and diligence to the others. Delitzsch notes that the verb is a denominative from the word for shoulder and properly means only to shoulder, that is, to make oneself ready, so that when early going forth is meant the word for morning generally stands with it. Wesley finds a moral in the haste: the church, having lost her beloved by former laziness, doubles her diligence. Gill has her take the first opportunity to visit the saints and learn their condition, and take Christ along so the visit is not in vain.

The vineyards themselves are read at two levels. Gill and Wesley both take them for particular congregations, gathered in order and distinguished from the world, and read the inspection of vine and pomegranate as inquiry into the success of their labours, what souls are brought in and how they grow. Clarke keeps the country in view, where they will have the better opportunity to observe the progress of spring, and notes her promise to be peculiarly affectionate to him there. Ellicott supplies philology: the clause on the tender grape appearing is literally that the vine blossoms open, and the word given as loves means caresses, where the Greek again read breasts.

What the mandrakes are is the one question nobody settles. Gill reports a long disagreement: some translate the word as lovely flowers, others take it for violets, others jessamine, others more probably lilies, on the grounds of season and place, fragrance and cup-like figure; one scholar contends the sense is that branches put forth sweet-smelling flowers, another extends that to fragrant flowers and fruits generally, and a third proposes an Arabian fruit. Wesley calls the meaning much doubted, settles on sweet and pleasant flowers, and allows that if mandrakes are meant they were of another sort than ours, since flowers of one kind differ across climates. Ellicott derives the word as love-apples, suggested by the word for loves just before and by the qualities ascribed to the plant. Clarke refers the reader to his note on the earlier passage and says the literal sense here, allowing for the concealing metaphors, is of a widely different nature from what is generally given, but leaves that to the reader's sagacity and prudence. On the fruits new and old, Wesley takes them for those of this year and the former, and reads them of the operations of the Spirit and degrees of grace in believers.
